title: Tavi and Drum and the Baker's Secret
markdown:
The town hugged itself: little houses with pointy roofs, flower boxes overflowing with giggling daisies, and Mrs. Crumbly’s bakery on the corner, where buns were softer than a baby dragon’s yawn and tastier than a rainbow. Each one was a cinnamon cloud. Lately they were famous for the wrong reason. Every morning a drift of pale, wispy wood shavings sat on the plumpest buns, as if someone had grated a pencil over breakfast. Scratchy. Confusing. Not a topping anyone had ordered.

Tavi, who lived with her toymaker uncle, popped in for her special weekend croissant and found Mrs. Crumbly sighing a floury cloud of sadness. “Oh dear, oh dear, Tavi. Look at this.”

Tavi looked. Her brain did a somersault. Who puts wood on a bun?

She reported to Drum, her alley-cat partner, on the bakery windowsill. Drum was fur as black as midnight and eyes like two shiny emeralds. He flicked his tail — a thoughtful flick, a this-needs-my-attention flick. He had smelled old socks and forgotten cheese. This was stranger.

“We have to figure this out,” Tavi said, chin in her hands, honey-coloured hair bouncing. “A weekend mystery. Involving buns. That’s the best kind.”

Drum leaped down with a soft thump you would not have heard a mouse sneeze over, and headed for the door as if jelly doughnuts were already at risk.

They began at the evidence bun Mrs. Crumbly had set aside. Tavi peered. “Look. A little shaving. A clue.” Drum sniffed, whiskers twitching like antennae. A faint smell of whittling. Cinnamon. Something metallic. Tavi giggled. “Whittling. You’re always sniffing out the best smells. Metallic. Interesting.”

They hid and waited. Tavi behind a sack of flour that smelled like warm hugs. Drum inside a shadow, which is a cat’s favourite room, blending with dust bunnies as if he had been invented there. It was Tuesday, but Tavi decided it felt like Saturday, because Saturdays were for adventures. A shadow flickered past the open back door. Then another. Quick as a blink.

“Did you see that?” Tavi whispered. Drum’s rumble said yes, and that it moved with haste.

They crept to the back door and tiptoed out. The air was roses and freshly cut grass — and there, just disappearing around the corner, a trail of tiny delicate shavings, like whispers from a very busy small pencil. They led down a narrow alley that smelled of socks forgotten for a week and, possibly, a grumpy badger’s lunch.

Tavi gasped and pointed. Drum was already ahead, tail a question mark. They scurried after the woody breadcrumb line, past bins that whispered secrets and graffiti that had sneezed paint. Fast. Exciting. Tavi was practically skipping.

A sound: waddle-waddle-waddle, not a march so much as a determined toddle. They peeked around crates that had seen a thousand alley years.

Not a person. Not a squirrel with a hobby. A clockwork duck: shiny brass, blue glass eyes like sapphires, tin feet doing the waddle. Under one wing, a secret pile of shavings. It was heading for a shed window left a crack open.

Tavi stuffed a laugh. “Why would a duck garnish buns?”

Drum’s eyes twinkled. The duck waddled only when it thought the alley was empty, apologetic as a shy teaspoon.

They watched it hop in. The window squeaked shut. Tavi and Drum put an eye to a door-crack. Workshop. Dust motes. Wood scraps. Tiny tools. In the middle sat the duck — Elbert, they later learned — attaching shavings to a small, elaborate wooden something that wanted to be a bird feeder, or a nest, or both.

“He’s making,” Tavi whispered.

Elbert quack-whirred, looked up, saw them, and clanked behind a workbench, mortified down to his tin toes.

Tavi opened the door as if it were a storybook. “Hello. We’re Tavi and Drum. We won’t hurt you. We only want the shavings.”

Elbert peeked, brass going faintly pink. A shy whir.

Drum rumbled the facts: buns, trail, detectives, case closed except the why.

Elbert looked at his tin toes, which tapped the floor in a nervous little dance. “I wanted to make something beautiful,” he confessed, clicks and whirrs like a music box winding down. “I’m a clockwork duck, but I love to make things. My uncle the toymaker makes toys that bring joy. I wanted a cozy wooden nest for the birds who sing outside my window every morning. They sound so cheerful. I used some of Mrs. Crumbly’s flour to help the wood stick. When I waddled home in the early light, the shavings must have fallen without me knowing.” He wrung his brass wings. “I just loved the smell of the buns. When I’m distracted by something so delicious, I get clumsy.”

Tavi’s heart melted like warm butter on a toasted bun. She stepped further in. “That’s not embarrassing at all. That’s wonderful. Presents for birds. Kind and thoughtful.”

Drum purred a deep rumble of approval, plus a polite note that next time, fewer shavings on the baked goods would delight the local bakers.

Tavi’s idea arrived with sparkle. “What if you helped Mrs. Crumbly? Official Shaving Sweeper. You’d be near all the yummy buns, you’d collect extras for nests, and she would always have perfectly clean icing. A win-win. A quack-win.”

Elbert’s beak opened. “I could help?”

Elbert’s blue eyes widened. “You mean it? I could help?”

“We certainly do,” Drum declared, tail flicking. They took him back along the shaving trail, which now looked less like a crime and more like a very small parade. Mrs. Crumbly, faced with a blushing brass duck and two detectives with flour on their knees, listened to the whole waddle of it. Then she handed Elbert a dustpan the size of a biscuit. He accepted it as if it were a medal.

Mrs. Crumbly was overjoyed in the specific way of someone whose icing had been restored to dignity. By the next morning the buns were legendary again, and only in the good way. Elbert waddled the bakery tiles with cheerful clink-clank, swept what he shed, and carried home enough pale curls for the coziest window-bird palaces in town. Tavi ate her croissant without a single crunch. Drum washed a paw on the sill, case filed under Kind and Crumbly. The alley kept its sock smell. The shed window stayed a little open, on purpose, so a clockwork duck could come and go with his treasures and leave the cinnamon to the cinnamon.
characters: Tavi (the toymaker's niece), Drum (an alley cat)
